title: Holding a note through a twelve-bar blues chorus
summary: Punch says he could hold a note for a chorus on trumpet, an idea from Joe Howard, unlike clarinetists.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Did you all take a long note and, you know, just hold a note?
I used to do that.
When?

Right here on his tongue. I remember we used to play, uh, the blues and I'd hold a note like I heard that client, they'd play a hold on it on that blues. I had a record there where a guy holds a note on the planet. I don't get his name. He's a white boy. No, I don't. Maybe he's white. I don't know.
Foster Bailey, I believe.
Oh, yeah.
He used to hold it with, uh, I can't think of the guy's name, but I know it. He's a bass player. That band he used to work with, the Charlie Shavers and Russell Crowe Colt.
You see them, the Klinex players, the Klinex players didn't hold a note to catch their breath.
Uh-huh.
No? No. No. No. No. But a band blowing a brass or something, he can't do that. He'd go to the end of his breath and cut out, see.
Well, how many bars could you hold it for in the blues? Any choruses?
I don't know, but I think I used to hold it more than four bars. Oh, yeah, way more than four.
For a chorus? Twelve bars?
Well, yeah, something like the blues. I could hold it from the beginning of a chorus to the end of the blues. That's twelve bars. Uh-huh. Yeah.
What tempo would that be? Can you tap it?
Hmm?
Tap that tempo or clap it with your hands that you'd hold that note. How fast would you be playing the blues?
Well, something like that. Like you'd be playing the blues and maybe the key of C. I see what you mean.
Mm-hmm. Well, I mean, when you were practicing awful long, right in the woodshed, would you ever hold a note like that?
Well, yeah, I used to do it on kind of headlong, you know, make you win long.
Mm-hmm.
I used to do it.
Who told you about that?
That's some of Joe Howard stuff. Mm-hmm.
